meeting_summary: Quick bridge call after last week's service degradation where a small fraction of requests experienced 10-60s tails. Focus: root cause hypotheses (KV-cache evictions, kernel fallbacks, autoscaler thrash), contractual exposure, and mitigation roadmap (dedicated hot path, fallback model variant, observability additions).
transcript:
[00:00:00] Ethan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we know this is urgent so we'll be concise. Meeting recorded at 15:30 UTC. Duration target ~45 minutes. Maya, you want to kick off?

[00:00:18] Maya (Redwood SE): Yeah, quick recap — we saw a long tail affecting ~0.8% of tokens which translated to about 0.3% of requests hitting 10-plus second latencies last Tuesday. Our early triage points to a mix of KV cache churn and a kernel fallback on certain sequence lengths. Apologies, I might say K-V cash sometimes in notes, my bad.

[00:00:45] Ravi (CTO, HelixPay): Thanks. From our side the big worry is that it coincided with settlement windows, so even if rare, it's customer visible. We also have contractual SLAs that trigger credits if p99 > 2s during a billing window — so we need a concrete mitigation path.

[00:01:10] Lena (SRE): I pulled the traces — most slow traces show a spike right after a cache eviction event. We suspect the autoscaler scaled down a small subset of instances and then a cold path took over. There's also some churn in our request size distribution that may be pushing those requests into a different kernel, maybe the bigger attention implementation.

[00:01:40] Maya (SE): Right, the runtime has a couple of heuristics: kernel selection by seq len, and fallback to more conservative kernels when memory pressure rises. If the model's kv cache can't be reused because of eviction, you get reprojection and extra work. Also there are retry loops in the client that make tails worse.

[00:02:12] Marissa (Product): Can you explain the kernel fallback in plain English? Our PMs keep asking if it's a config we can change or a code thing.

[00:02:26] Maya: Sure — think of it as two implementations: fast-specialized kernels for the common-case sequences, and a slower, more robust kernel for edge-case lengths or when quantization paths mismatch. Switching between them is automatic. We can tune the thresholds but that risks correctness if we force the fast path.

[00:02:52] Omar (Infra): We also saw a spike in cold-starts for a small pool. Is that autoscaler oscillation? Our infra shows pods terminated around T-80s before the spike.

[00:03:05] Ethan (AE): To be explicit about options: short term we can propose a Dedicated hot-path with reserved capacity for your settlement windows; mid-term we can push kernel threshold tuning + improved KV caching heuristics; long term we can add per-customer routing to fallback model variants with smaller memory footprint.

[00:03:36] Ravi: Dedicated makes sense but cost is a concern. Also need to know rollback and fail-open behaviour — we can't have silent failures during peak.

[00:03:48] Maya: Understood. We can do a canary dedicated pool for the 2-hour settlement window (burst reservation) so cost is limited. And we'll provide an automatic fallback to a verified smaller model that preserves semantics for critical endpoints — that'll cap latencies, lower quality delta is measurable.

[00:04:12] Lena: We need auditability too — we must show exactly which requests were served by which variant for compliance. Does the platform provide per-request trace IDs we can map?

[00:04:26] Tom (CSM): Yes, we'll send the trace schema and a sample CSV export. Also Redwood Console already surfaces per-route token/token-cost and per-request traces — we'll include example links (e.g., https://redwood.ai/console/traces/EXAMPLE).

[00:04:45] Marissa: There was also talk internally about encryption and keys — if we move to Dedicated, how does KMS integrate? Our security folks will need HSM or customer-managed KMS.

[00:04:58] Maya: Dedicated and Private both support external KMS, yes. We'll attach the security packet — SOC2, ISO notes, KMS integration docs: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2 and https://redwood.ai/docs/kms.

[00:05:20] Ravi: Good. On the SLA crediting front, we need a proposal that doesn't break our renewal math.

[00:05:28] Ethan: We're drafting an interim crediting proposal that is targeted to incidents with measurable p99 deviation and limited to customer-impact windows. I'll send language by end of week.

[00:05:40] Lena: Back to the technical root cause — can Redwood share the slow-path kernel logs and the exact sequence-length distribution for the affected requests?

[00:05:52] Maya: Yes — action item for me to extract kernel-selection traces and KV cache hit-rate over the incident window. We'll also trim the traces for PII before sharing.

[00:06:05] Marissa: We can run a synthetic against a dedicated pool if you give us the runner config. We need to validate that the dedicated path removes the tail entirely.

[00:06:18] Omar: Also want to test network flakiness scenarios — we had one case where midflight connection hiccup coincided with a fallback and made things worse.

[00:06:30] Maya: We'll include a test script that simulates dropped connections and cache invalidation scenarios.

[00:06:42] Ethan: For transparency, we'll also surface the unit economics: token cost delta for dedicated vs hosted during the settlement window so you can quantify tradeoffs.

[00:06:55] Ravi: Sounds good. I want to flag contractual exposure again — if we can't get a reliable p99 under 2s we need to discuss credits, but prefer engineering mitigations first.

[00:07:08] Lena: Quick question on observability: can we add an alert for sudden shift in kernel mix or kv cache miss rate? That would help us beat the tail proactively.

[00:07:20] Maya: Yes, Redwood Console exposes metric streams for kernel-selection ratios and cache-hit rates. We can suggest an alert rule (we'll attach playbook).

[00:07:33] Marissa: Any immediate configuration changes we should avoid? We tried bumping token limit on client and that actually increased tail due to more retries.

[00:07:44] Maya: Recommend against client-side aggressive retries without jitter. We'll send client tuning guidance.

[00:07:55] Ethan: Let's walk through the proposed mitigation plan timeline: (1) Share trimmed traces + kernel logs (Maya) by 09-22; (2) HelixPay to run synthetic load versus a dedicated small pool by 09-26; (3) Canary in production for settlement window using reserve burst capacity by 09-29; (4) If canary passes, formalize dedicated commit or routing fallback.

[00:08:28] Ravi: That timeline is OK. Will you include an interim credit proposal in step (1) so we have contract language?

[00:08:37] Ethan: Yep, draft SLA language and the crediting approach included in the email.

[00:08:45] Lena: Minor nit — when you share traces, can you include the client-side request IDs? We need end-to-end mapping.

[00:08:53] Maya: We'll keep request IDs, but we'll mask PII. Also we'll include an example mapping table.

[00:09:06] Marissa: What about regression monitoring — say a future model update changes kernel profiles. How do we prevent reintroducing this?

[00:09:16] Maya: We recommend adding a nightly eval that includes the long-tail prompt set. Redwood Optimize can run regression checks and alert on q99 latency regressions tied to a prompt set. We'll share the eval config as part of the artifact bundle.

[00:09:34] Omar: One security question — if we go Dedicated, can we have per-instance audit logs shipped to our SIEM?

[00:09:44] Tom (CSM): Yes, we support log-forwarding and audit exports; will include a sample ingest config for Splunk/Datadog.

[00:09:55] Ravi: OK thanks. Anything else on the technical front?

[00:10:02] Ethan: I want to make sure we captured the risk: this is a low-frequency but high-severity tail tied to cache eviction and kernel fallback amplified by client retry patterns. Mitigations: short-term reserved bursts, client retry tuning, medium-term kernel threshold tuning + improved caching heuristics, long-term per-customer routing and smaller verified variants.

[00:10:30] Marissa: Also request a short post-incident summary we can share with our execs focused on impact, remediation, and next steps.

[00:10:40] Tom: We'll produce that — concise one-pager with timeline and mitigations.

[00:10:48] Ethan: Great. Final check: any blockers to the plan from HelixPay?

[00:10:55] Ravi: None immediate. Just need the credit proposal early.

[00:11:02] Lena: And the kernel logs.

[00:11:05] Maya: On it.

[00:11:08] Ethan: Ok we wrapped earlier than planned. We'll follow up via email and put artifacts in the shared drive (links). Thanks all.

[00:11:18] (meeting end)

Notes: transcript contains some ASR mistakes (company names, acronyms). References: security packet link, console trace sample link.
